title: Correct Answers But No Learning
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick uses a small domestic moment - his daughter breezing through a phonics puzzle by matching colours rather than blending sounds - to build a broader argument about the deceptiveness of task completion as a proxy for learning. He diagnoses the puzzle's 'fatal flaw' as an instructional-design failure: its surface features (colour-coding) were more salient and easier to exploit than its intended cognitive target (phoneme blending), so his daughter succeeded at the task while never actually practising the skill it was meant to build. Drawing on Paul Kirschner's definition of learning as a change in long-term memory, and Robert Bjork's concept of 'illusions of comprehension and competence,' Hendrick argues his daughter experienced a satisfying but false sense of mastery - and generalises this into a pointed scepticism toward 'engagement' as an educational metric, since a child can be busy, enthusiastic, and producing correct answers while learning nothing of value. He grounds the argument in Craik and Lockhart's classic levels-of-processing research (shallow, perceptual processing produces weaker memories than deep, meaning-based processing) and Chi and Glaser's novice-expert studies, arguing that repeated exposure to poorly-designed tasks doesn't just fail to build deep understanding - it actively trains students in what he calls 'expertise in superficiality,' sophisticated strategies for succeeding at tasks while bypassing the cognitive work they were meant to promote. His closing claim reframes instructional design as never neutral: every task teaches something, whether by design or by accident, and the only real question is whether it's teaching the intended thing.
points: Hendrick's central diagnostic moment: his daughter completed a phonics blending puzzle correctly by matching colours rather than blending sounds, revealing that the task's surface features were more salient than its intended cognitive target.

His key framing, via Paul Kirschner: learning is a change in long-term memory, so a task that produces correct answers without engaging the intended cognitive process leaves the relevant memory 'essentially untouched,' regardless of how well the student performed.

He invokes Robert Bjork's 'illusions of comprehension and competence' to explain why these surface-level victories feel so convincing to both student and teacher - the task felt successful because it was easy and produced correct answers.

His resulting scepticism toward 'engagement' as an effectiveness metric: a child who is busy, enthusiastic, and producing correct responses 'may be learning nothing of value,' and may even be reinforcing counterproductive shortcuts.

His sharpest coined phrase, 'expertise in superficiality': repeated exposure to poorly-designed tasks doesn't just fail to build deep understanding, it actively trains students in sophisticated strategies for succeeding while bypassing the cognitive work the task was meant to promote.
quotes: When I asked her how she was doing so well in making the words and to talk me through her strategy, she said: "You just match the colours, Dad.

The surface features of the task (colour-matching) are more salient than the underlying cognitive goal (phoneme blending). She completed the task correctly, but without actually practising the skill it was supposed to develop.
My daughter experienced what Robert Bjork call "illusions of comprehension and competence": the misleading sense that she had mastered the skill when she had merely found a workaround.

This is why we should be deeply sceptical of "engagement" as a metric for educational effectiveness. A child who is busily occupied, enthusiastically participating, and producing correct responses may be learning nothing of value.
Learning doesn't always happen when the student completes a task. It's what happens when the task causes the student to think. Instructional design is not neutral, it always teaches something.
